We have discussed DeepMind’s earlier triumphs: teaching machines to master video games, beat the best Go players alive, and generate humanlike conversation. But this time, the target was not language or strategy. It was biology. One of the great mysteries in molecular biology has been protein folding. Proteins are the workhorses of biology—responsible for almost everything that happens inside a living cell. But proteins don’t function as simple strings. They must twist, fold, and contort into complex three-dimensional shapes in order to do their work. 107 And understanding how a protein folds has been a monumental challenge. You will recall that this was called AlphaFold, and for this work, Demis Hassabis from Google won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024. 108 A Backstory on Protein Research One of the most visionary minds I’ve had the privilege to call a very close friend is Dr. Larry Gold, the founder of SomaLogic and a true pioneer in the molecular sciences. 109 His work is incredibly sophisticated, steeped in an advanced understanding of the nuance and mechanics of biology, and deeply rewarding to explore. Larry’s work has shaped much of what we now understand about how proteins can be measured and interpreted—not just as biochemical artifacts but as a living, dynamic record of what’s happening in the body. Through SomaLogic, he developed technologies that can measure thousands of proteins in a single drop of blood, offering a time-lapse view into human biology. 110 What makes Larry’s thinking so compelling is his insistence on treating biology as information. DNA is not a blueprint in the conventional sense. It’s an instruction set—code that unfolds not statically, but dynamically, through time. From this code come proteins, which then twist, fold, and assemble to build the body itself. The sequence becomes shape. The shape becomes function. And the function becomes life. After scientists successfully mapped human DNA, it was Larry who began the intense work of mapping the proteome that follows it. 111 Larry is the godfather of the field of proteome research, which is studying the proteins in your body—these are produced from your DNA but constantly shift in response to your body’s needs and conditions. Your DNA can give a clue as to what cancer or other condition you might get; once you can map your proteome, you can detect what cancer or other condition you have . For Larry, the goal was to be able to determine this from a simple urine sample, long before traditional methods could detect it. And early detection means much higher rates of cure. There is a building at the University of Colorado in Boulder, sitting just above my home, that originally opened in 1995 as the Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology Building and was renamed the Gold Biosciences Building in 2013 to honor Larry’s significant contributions to the field of biosciences. He is crazy smart, for sure. But I love him because he is incredibly funny and is a kind and patient teacher and friend. Just as our brains are born not with knowledge but with a learning architecture, our biology is born not with a finished product, but with a deeply encoded capacity for construction. The parallels between cognition and biology—as dynamic systems shaped by feedback, constraint, and information—are striking to me. And that’s why what came next was so extraordinary. AlphaFold: Solving One of Life’s Most Intriguing Puzzles The rules of protein folding are governed by physics, but the possibilities are astronomical. Predicting the final shape of even a modestly sized protein requires understanding a dizzying interplay of atomic forces. According to what is called Levinthal’s paradox, a protein chain has so many possible configurations (estimated at 10 300 ) that if it tried them all sequentially to find the right shape, it would take longer than the age of the universe, yet our biological systems do it in milliseconds. 112 And then came AlphaFold. Using deep learning and neural networks, AlphaFold learned to predict the 3D structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences with astonishing accuracy—sometimes to the atomic level. 113 It didn’t just match human scientists. It partnered with them to make a huge leap forward. While the wet-lab work takes months or years, AlphaFold can generate a prediction in minutes or seconds. DeepMind has since released the predicted structures of nearly all known proteins, over two hundred million, to the public—a feat that would have taken hundreds of millions of years using human-only methods. 114 AlphaFold can now be used to engineer more resilient crops for a warmer climate, tackle heart disease, target early-onset Parkinson’s disease, create plastic-eating enzymes to reduce the impact of plastic pollution, and address other challenges. 115 It is now being used by two million researchers in over 190 countries. 116 Andrei Lupas, an evolutionary biologist and CASP judge, famously said after seeing AlphaFold’s results: “This will change medicine. It will change research. It will change bioengineering. It will change everything.” 117 The organizers of CASP officially declared the challenge of predicting single-protein structures “solved.” 118 The protein folding problem, one of the holy grails of biology, had been cracked—not by a biologist alone, but in partnership with an AI neural network. Intelligence Advancing Biology Demis Hassabis (CEO of Google’s DeepMind) approaches biology as an information processing system. 119 If even biology is information at its core, the implications for AI driving advancements in human quality of life are spectacular. Already, scientists are beginning to use AlphaFold’s breakthroughs for the possible acceleration of drug discovery, personalized medicine, and precision cancer treatments. In one promising development, researchers have begun designing custom proteins that might be able to target the unique mutations in an individual’s cancer. 120 Not generic medicine—tailored molecules, custom-built to fit a single person’s biology.
